articles.title: Record-breaking sightings of rare moth in Essex
articles.summary: There is now a self-sustaining population of the moth at a nature reserve in Essex, a charity says.
articles.content:
Wildlife enthusiasts have made a record-breaking number of sightings of an elusive moth at a nature reserve.

The Fisher's estuarine moth has been spotted 111 times at Abbotts Hall in Great Wigborough, near Colchester, in 2026.

Dr Zoe Ringwood, of Essex Wildlife Trust, said work to boost the highly threatened species' population had been an "important success story".

The charity has pledged to continue surveying new and existing plots on the Essex coast.

Fisher's estuarine moths can be recognised by their pale gold-brown wing colour with light and dark spots, and are naturally found in low-lying areas of natural grassland which are vulnerable to erosion.

They are reliant on rare hog's fennel for their survival, but the plant has been affected by rising sea levels.

To protect the species, Essex Wildlife Trust planted hog's fennel at Abbotts Hall in 2005 and introduced moth eggs five years later.
articles.reasoning: The article reports a successful conservation effort resulting in a self-sustaining population of a highly threatened moth species, which has broad ecological significance and demonstrates effective environmental stewardship.
articles.personality_title: Rare moth population thrives in Essex nature reserve
articles.personality_presentation:
**Context** – The Fisher's estuarine moth is a rare insect that lives in low-lying grasslands near the coast. It depends on a special plant called hog's fennel, which has been threatened by rising sea levels.

**What happened** – In 2026, wildlife watchers spotted the Fisher's estuarine moth 111 times at Abbotts Hall nature reserve near Colchester, Essex. This is the highest number of sightings ever recorded there. The Essex Wildlife Trust started planting hog's fennel in 2005 and introduced moth eggs in 2010 to help the moth survive.

**Impact** – This is an important success because the moth was once highly threatened and hard to find. Now, a healthy, self-sustaining population lives at the reserve. This shows that careful conservation work, like planting the right plants and protecting habitats, can help endangered species recover.

**What's next step** – The Essex Wildlife Trust plans to keep checking the moth population and its habitat along the Essex coast. They want to protect more areas and learn how to help the moth and other species continue to thrive.

**One-sentence takeaway** – Careful planting and protection helped a rare moth species build a strong population in Essex for the first time in many years.
articles.personality_title_fr: Une population rare de papillons de nuit prospère dans une réserve naturelle d'Essex
articles.personality_presentation_fr:
**Contexte** – Le papillon de nuit estuarien de Fisher est un insecte rare qui vit dans les prairies basses près de la côte. Il dépend d'une plante spéciale appelée fenouil des marais, menacée par la montée du niveau de la mer.

**Ce qui s'est passé** – En 2026, les observateurs de la faune ont repéré le papillon de nuit estuarien de Fisher 111 fois dans la réserve naturelle d'Abbotts Hall près de Colchester, Essex. C'est le nombre le plus élevé jamais enregistré à cet endroit. L'Essex Wildlife Trust a commencé à planter du fenouil des marais en 2005 et a introduit des œufs de papillons en 2010 pour aider l'espèce.

**Impact** – C'est un succès important car ce papillon était autrefois très menacé et difficile à trouver. Aujourd'hui, une population saine et autonome vit dans la réserve. Cela montre que des actions de conservation bien pensées, comme planter les bonnes plantes et protéger les habitats, peuvent aider les espèces en danger à se rétablir.

**Prochaine étape** – L'Essex Wildlife Trust prévoit de continuer à surveiller la population de papillons et leur habitat le long de la côte d'Essex. Ils veulent protéger plus de zones et apprendre comment aider cette espèce et d'autres à prospérer.

**Résumé en une phrase** – La plantation et la protection soigneuses ont permis à une espèce rare de papillon de nuit de construire une population forte en Essex pour la première fois depuis de nombreuses années.
articles.personality_title_es: Población rara de polilla prospera en reserva natural de Essex
articles.personality_presentation_es:
**Contexto** – La polilla estuarina de Fisher es un insecto raro que vive en pastizales bajos cerca de la costa. Depende de una planta especial llamada hinojo de pantano, que está amenazada por la subida del nivel del mar.

**Qué pasó** – En 2026, observadores de la vida silvestre vieron la polilla estuarina de Fisher 111 veces en la reserva natural Abbotts Hall cerca de Colchester, Essex. Este es el número más alto de avistamientos registrado allí. La organización Essex Wildlife Trust comenzó a plantar hinojo de pantano en 2005 y a introducir huevos de polilla en 2010 para ayudar a la especie.

**Impacto** – Esto es un éxito importante porque la polilla estaba muy amenazada y era difícil de encontrar. Ahora, una población saludable y autosuficiente vive en la reserva. Esto muestra que el trabajo cuidadoso de conservación, como plantar las plantas correctas y proteger el hábitat, puede ayudar a que especies en peligro se recuperen.

**Próximos pasos** – Essex Wildlife Trust planea seguir monitoreando la población de polillas y su hábitat a lo largo de la costa de Essex. Quieren proteger más áreas y aprender cómo ayudar a esta y otras especies a prosperar.

**Resumen en una frase** – La plantación y protección cuidadosa ayudaron a que una especie rara de polilla construyera una población fuerte en Essex por primera vez en muchos años.

articles.title: New net-zero community will become Michigan’s first virtual power plant
articles.content:
Mitch Hall and his wife, Lori, live in one of the most sustainable communities in the U.S. Their town house is among a few dozen residences constructed so far at Veridian at County Farm, a fossil-fuel-free, net-zero-energy development in Ann Arbor, Michigan. Homes here make about as much solar energy as they consume, with the help of batteries that save solar power for use in the evenings.

Now, the couple is eager to share the benefits of their clean energy infrastructure with the wider grid.

In the coming weeks, Veridian households can enroll in Michigan’s first residential pilot of a virtual power plant; Detroit-based utility DTE Energy will then be able to remotely control the network of residents’ home batteries to inject their stored solar power onto the grid when operators need it most.

“This pilot is an opportunity to test an approach that could ultimately provide a lower-cost way to meet growing energy needs and strengthen reliability,” Joi Harris, president and chief executive officer of DTE Energy, said in a statement. VPPs can smooth out demand peaks, reducing the utility’s need to invest in grid-infrastructure upgrades and generate kilowatt-hours with expensive fossil fuel peaker plants, both of which would pile costs on consumers.

To support our nonprofit environmental journalism, please consider disabling your ad-blocker to allow ads on Grist. Here's How

The initiative ​“should work well for the residents, too,” Hall said. ​“DTE will pay us a little bit to be part of this project.” Because the utility will pull battery power automatically when the grid is strained and electricity prices are likely to be highest, ​“a neat part about the virtual power plant is you don’t have to spend a lot of time learning and trying to optimize,” he noted. ​“DTE will manage that battery for you.” (DTE did not respond to Canary Media’s request for exact figures on how much it would compensate customers in time for publication.)

VPPs have existed for years but have been slow to gain widespread traction because of a host of factors. Utilities often haven’t been incentivized to embrace the approach, while home solar and batteries remain too expensive for many households in the U.S. But as electrification and the data center rush spur unprecedented demand, VPPs are taking off as a fast way to get power on the grid. Earlier this month, the Brattle Group estimated that 524 gigawatts of distributed energy resources harnessed in VPPs could save households on average $122 per year by 2050.

Currently, ​“there’s immense untapped capacity,” said Kevin Brehm, manager in the carbon-free electricity practice at clean energy think tank RMI.

Matt Grocoff, the founder of Thrive Collaborative, started to consider a VPP pilot at Veridian in 2019. He wanted the neighborhood to mimic an ecosystem — a resilient web of relationships in which individual organisms do more than just extract resources. For example, a tree in a forest turns sunlight into nutrients and shares them symbiotically with a vast, interconnected underground web of fungi.

To support our nonprofit environmental journalism, please consider disabling your ad-blocker to allow ads on Grist. Here's How

Likewise, with a VPP, each Veridian home ​“can be producing energy that it needs and mutually beneficially sharing it across a network of energy rather than a linear grid that flows in only one direction,” Grocoff said.

DTE expects nearly 100 battery-equipped Veridian homes to ultimately participate in the pilot. So far, 44 market-rate homes with solar and batteries have been built, out of 120 planned, as have 50 affordable housing units that don’t have batteries yet, according to Thrive Collaborative. Battery manufacturer Sonnen USA, maker of the home storage systems installed at Veridian, is helping DTE operate the pilot using Sonnen’s proprietary software.

“Veridian is a test bed,” said Geoff Ferrell, executive vice president of Sonnen USA’s VPP business unit. The initiative, which is expected to be able to deliver up to about 300 kilowatts for three hours, will give DTE a clearer picture of how much power the home battery fleet can actually generate and when, providing ​“a really great basis” for a scaled-up program, he noted.

Ferrell points to another Sonnen-facilitated VPP that also sprang up as a humble pilot project, but rapidly mushroomed into a full-scale program because of early positive results. That initiative started in 2017 with a new apartment building topped with solar, Soleil Lofts outside Salt Lake City.

Sonnen hadn’t even finished installing batteries in each of the development’s 600 units when the utility Rocky Mountain Power and the state utility commission decided that the initial data was promising enough to merit extending the program to every residential customer in the utility’s territory, Ferrell said. Today, about 7,900 homes and businesses participate in the program, now called Wattsmart Battery, in Utah, Wyoming, and Idaho.

Given the success of that VPP and many others, Brehm would like to see more utilities go full throttle at the outset.

“Do you need another pilot?” he asked, noting that numerous VPP programs exist for utilities to model their own programs after.

But for utilities that do approach VPPs with caution, Rocky Mountain Power’s pilot is a good model, according to Brehm. The utility’s employees were able to rapidly understand how the residential battery fleet worked and how to deploy it, he said, ​“so that they could integrate these batteries into their operations initially, and subsequently [into their resource-capacity] planning.” He’d like to see DTE do the same.

The VPP pilot at Veridian is already starting to inspire developers and utilities outside Michigan, including the development Peace Hill in Townsend, Washington, said Grocoff of Thrive Collaborative.

“We’re getting calls from all over the country,” Grocoff said. ​“It’s really exciting.”
articles.reasoning: The article reports on Michigan's first virtual power plant pilot in a net-zero-energy community, which has broad positive environmental impact by promoting renewable energy use, grid reliability, and cost savings for consumers. The story provides detailed context about the technology, the community involved, and the potential for scaling, making it a substantial and inspiring example of clean energy innovation with meaningful societal benefits.
articles.personality_title: Michigan launches first virtual power plant in a net-zero community
articles.personality_presentation:
**Context** – In Ann Arbor, Michigan, a new community called Veridian at County Farm is built to be very environmentally friendly. The homes there produce as much solar energy as they use, storing extra power in batteries for nighttime use.

**What happened** – Soon, nearly 100 homes in Veridian will join Michigan’s first virtual power plant (VPP) pilot. This means the local utility, DTE Energy, can remotely control the home batteries to send stored solar power back to the electric grid when it’s needed most.

**Impact** – This virtual power plant can help reduce the need for expensive power plants that use fossil fuels and cut costs for both the utility and its customers. Homeowners like Mitch Hall will even get paid a little for sharing their stored energy. The system makes managing energy simple because the utility handles when to use the batteries, so residents don’t have to do anything.

**What’s next step** – DTE Energy will learn from this pilot how to best use home batteries on a bigger scale. If successful, more communities and utilities across the country might adopt similar programs, helping to make power grids cleaner and more reliable.

**One-sentence takeaway** – Michigan’s new virtual power plant pilot shows how neighborhoods with solar batteries can work together to provide clean, affordable energy to the grid when it’s needed most.
articles.personality_title_fr: Le Michigan lance sa première centrale électrique virtuelle dans une communauté zéro énergie
articles.personality_presentation_fr:
**Contexte** – À Ann Arbor, dans le Michigan, une nouvelle communauté appelée Veridian at County Farm est conçue pour être très respectueuse de l’environnement. Les maisons produisent autant d’énergie solaire qu’elles en consomment, en stockant l’excédent dans des batteries pour la nuit.

**Ce qui s’est passé** – Bientôt, près de 100 maisons de Veridian participeront au premier projet pilote de centrale électrique virtuelle (VPP) du Michigan. Cela signifie que le fournisseur d’énergie local, DTE Energy, pourra contrôler à distance les batteries domestiques pour renvoyer l’énergie solaire stockée vers le réseau électrique quand elle est la plus nécessaire.

**Impact** – Cette centrale électrique virtuelle peut aider à réduire le besoin de centrales coûteuses utilisant des combustibles fossiles et à diminuer les coûts pour le fournisseur et ses clients. Les habitants comme Mitch Hall seront même rémunérés pour partager leur énergie stockée. Le système facilite la gestion de l’énergie, car le fournisseur décide quand utiliser les batteries, donc les résidents n’ont rien à faire.

**Prochaine étape** – DTE Energy va apprendre de ce projet pilote comment mieux utiliser les batteries domestiques à plus grande échelle. En cas de succès, davantage de communautés et de fournisseurs d’énergie à travers le pays pourraient adopter des programmes similaires, rendant les réseaux électriques plus propres et fiables.

**En une phrase** – Le projet pilote de centrale électrique virtuelle du Michigan montre comment des quartiers avec des batteries solaires peuvent collaborer pour fournir une énergie propre et abordable au réseau quand c’est le plus nécessaire.
articles.personality_title_es: Michigan lanza su primera planta de energía virtual en una comunidad de energía cero neto
articles.personality_presentation_es:
**Contexto** – En Ann Arbor, Michigan, una nueva comunidad llamada Veridian at County Farm está construida para ser muy respetuosa con el medio ambiente. Las casas producen tanta energía solar como consumen, almacenando el exceso en baterías para usar por la noche.

**Qué pasó** – Pronto, casi 100 hogares en Veridian participarán en la primera planta de energía virtual (VPP) piloto de Michigan. Esto significa que la compañía eléctrica local, DTE Energy, podrá controlar remotamente las baterías del hogar para enviar la energía solar almacenada a la red eléctrica cuando más se necesite.

**Impacto** – Esta planta de energía virtual puede ayudar a reducir la necesidad de plantas de energía costosas que usan combustibles fósiles y disminuir costos para la compañía y sus clientes. Los residentes como Mitch Hall incluso recibirán un pago por compartir su energía almacenada. El sistema facilita el manejo de la energía porque la compañía decide cuándo usar las baterías, por lo que los residentes no tienen que hacer nada.

**Próximos pasos** – DTE Energy aprenderá de este piloto cómo usar mejor las baterías domésticas a mayor escala. Si tiene éxito, más comunidades y compañías eléctricas en todo el país podrían adoptar programas similares, ayudando a que las redes eléctricas sean más limpias y confiables.

**Una frase clave** – El piloto de planta de energía virtual de Michigan muestra cómo vecindarios con baterías solares pueden trabajar juntos para proporcionar energía limpia y asequible a la red cuando más se necesita.

articles.title: Hormuz swim highlights environmental cost of war
articles.summary: Ocean campaigner Lewis Pugh completes Hormuz challenge and warns of lasting environmental damage.
articles.content:
A British endurance swimmer has completed a three-day swim through the Strait of Hormuz to draw attention to what he says is the environmental cost of the conflict involving Iran.

Lewis Pugh, who is a UN Patron of the Oceans, swam about 15km (9.3 miles) through the strategic waterway, a key route for oil shipments from the Middle East.

Pugh, 56, who was born in Plymouth, Devon said "war causes immense human suffering" but nature is "another casualty that receives far too little attention".

He is calling for an end to the fighting, the reopening of the Strait of Hormuz and action to address environmental damage caused by the conflict.
articles.reasoning: The article highlights a high-profile environmental awareness campaign by a UN Patron of the Oceans, focusing on the significant environmental damage caused by conflict in a globally strategic waterway. The swim draws meaningful attention to the environmental cost of war, urging action that could benefit ecosystems and global environmental health.
articles.personality_title: Swimmer highlights environmental damage in Strait of Hormuz
articles.personality_presentation:
**Context** – The Strait of Hormuz is a narrow waterway between the Persian Gulf and the Arabian Sea. It is very important because many oil shipments from the Middle East pass through it. Recently, the area has been affected by conflict involving Iran, which has caused damage to the environment.

**What happened** – Lewis Pugh, a British swimmer and UN Patron of the Oceans, completed a three-day swim covering about 15 kilometers (9.3 miles) across the Strait of Hormuz. His swim took place to show how war in this region harms the natural environment, not just people.

**Impact** – Pugh’s swim brings attention to the fact that war causes serious environmental problems that people often forget. By swimming through this key waterway, he highlighted the lasting damage caused by fighting, which can affect marine life and the health of the ocean. This focus helps people understand that protecting nature is also important during conflicts.

**What’s next step** – Pugh is asking for the fighting to stop and for the Strait of Hormuz to be reopened safely. He also wants governments and groups to work on fixing the environmental damage caused by the conflict. His swim may inspire new efforts to protect and restore this important area.

**One-sentence takeaway** – A British swimmer’s journey through the Strait of Hormuz shines a light on the hidden environmental harm caused by war and calls for urgent action to protect this vital waterway.
articles.personality_title_fr: Un nageur met en lumière les dégâts environnementaux dans le détroit d’Hormuz
articles.personality_presentation_fr:
**Contexte** – Le détroit d’Hormuz est un passage étroit entre le golfe Persique et la mer d’Arabie. Il est très important car de nombreuses cargaisons de pétrole du Moyen-Orient y transitent. Récemment, cette zone a été touchée par un conflit impliquant l’Iran, causant des dégâts à l’environnement.

**Ce qui s’est passé** – Lewis Pugh, nageur britannique et Parrain des Océans pour l’ONU, a nagé pendant trois jours environ 15 kilomètres à travers le détroit d’Hormuz. Sa traversée avait pour but de montrer que la guerre dans cette région nuit à la nature, pas seulement aux humains.

**Impact** – La nage de Pugh attire l’attention sur le fait que la guerre cause des problèmes environnementaux graves souvent oubliés. En nageant dans ce passage stratégique, il a souligné les dégâts durables causés par les combats, qui peuvent affecter la vie marine et la santé des océans. Cela aide à comprendre que protéger la nature est aussi important en temps de conflit.

**Prochaine étape** – Pugh demande l’arrêt des combats et la réouverture sécurisée du détroit d’Hormuz. Il souhaite aussi que les gouvernements et organisations travaillent à réparer les dommages environnementaux causés par le conflit. Sa nage pourrait inspirer de nouvelles actions pour protéger et restaurer cette zone clé.

**Résumé en une phrase** – Le parcours d’un nageur britannique dans le détroit d’Hormuz met en lumière les dégâts environnementaux cachés causés par la guerre et appelle à agir rapidement pour protéger cette voie maritime vitale.
articles.personality_title_es: Nadador destaca daños ambientales en el estrecho de Ormuz
articles.personality_presentation_es:
**Contexto** – El estrecho de Ormuz es un paso estrecho entre el Golfo Pérsico y el Mar Arábigo. Es muy importante porque por allí pasan muchos envíos de petróleo desde Medio Oriente. Recientemente, la zona ha estado afectada por un conflicto que involucra a Irán, causando daños al medio ambiente.

**Qué pasó** – Lewis Pugh, un nadador británico y Patrocinador de los Océanos de la ONU, completó una travesía de tres días nadando aproximadamente 15 kilómetros (9.3 millas) a través del estrecho de Ormuz. Su objetivo era mostrar cómo la guerra en esa región daña la naturaleza, no solo a las personas.

**Impacto** – La natación de Pugh llama la atención sobre el hecho de que la guerra causa graves problemas ambientales que muchas veces se olvidan. Al nadar por esta vía estratégica, destacó el daño duradero causado por el conflicto, que puede afectar la vida marina y la salud del océano. Esto ayuda a que la gente entienda que proteger la naturaleza también es importante durante las guerras.

**Próximo paso** – Pugh pide que se detengan los combates y que se reabra el estrecho de Ormuz de forma segura. También quiere que gobiernos y grupos trabajen para reparar los daños ambientales causados por el conflicto. Su natación puede inspirar nuevos esfuerzos para proteger y restaurar esta zona importante.

**Resumen en una frase** – El recorrido de un nadador británico por el estrecho de Ormuz revela el daño ambiental oculto causado por la guerra y llama a actuar con urgencia para proteger esta vía vital.
